opus-5.5.text:
I think the key shift is moving from a model that just answers in one shot to a model that actually *does work* over a long horizon. In the traditional setup, you give the model a question, it thinks, and it produces an answer. The information it can use is fixed at the start. But with an agent, the model takes an action, like searching, running code, or calling a tool. Then it gets feedback from the environment, updates its understanding, and decides what to do next. So the problem is solved through a loop, not in a single pass.

Why does this matter? Many real-world tasks simply can't be solved with the information the model has in its weights or in the initial prompt. You need to go out and get new information. You need to try something, see that it fails, and adjust. That's very close to how humans actually work. When a researcher or an engineer solves a hard problem, they don't sit there and produce the final answer from pure reasoning. They experiment, they read, they debug. The intelligence shows up in how well you use that feedback.

From a technical perspective, a few things become really important. The first is long context, or more precisely, long-horizon reasoning. If an agent interacts with the environment dozens or hundreds of times, the trajectory gets very long, and the model has to keep track of what it has tried, what it learned, and what the current goal is. This is one reason we cared about long context from very early on. It's not just about reading a long document. It's the foundation for the model to have a working memory over a long task.

The second is that the training paradigm changes. With pretraining, you're basically learning from static human data. But for agents, a lot of the capability has to come from reinforcement learning in environments, where the model gets a reward for actually completing the task. The model learns strategies that aren't necessarily written down anywhere in human text, like when to verify, when to backtrack, and when to search more versus when to commit. In a sense, the environment becomes a new source of data. As high-quality human data becomes relatively scarce, I think this kind of interaction-generated data becomes one of the main drivers of progress.

The third is robustness. In a single-turn setting, a small mistake just gives you a slightly worse answer. But in a multi-step setting, errors compound. If each step has some chance of going wrong, a long task can fail entirely. So the model needs to be able to notice its own errors and recover from them. That's a different kind of ability from just being knowledgeable.

So my understanding is that multi-round interaction is really how a model's intelligence gets turned into actual productivity. The model's reasoning ability is like the engine, but the interaction with the outside world is what lets it do real tasks, the kind that might take a human hours or even days. I think that's where a lot of the value of AI over the next few years is going to come from.

r001.rationale: It says the agent receives environmental feedback, updates its understanding, and decides what to do next.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is that an agent is a model that's been given the ability to act, observe, and then act again. In a single-turn setting, the model takes all the information it has and produces one answer. Whether that answer is right or wrong, the episode is over. In a multi-turn setting, the model does something, the world responds, and that response becomes new information the model didn't have before. So the key difference isn't really the number of steps. It's that the model can acquire information it didn't start with.

That changes the nature of the problem quite a lot. A lot of real tasks simply can't be solved from the initial prompt alone. If you ask me to fix a bug in a codebase, I don't know what's in the codebase. I have to look. If I search for something, I don't know what the search will return. The only way to make progress is to interact, see what comes back, update my understanding, and decide what to do next. In that sense, a multi-turn agent is doing something closer to what a person does at work. You form a hypothesis, you test it, you're often wrong, and you adjust.

The interesting part, from a training perspective, is that this makes the problem long-horizon. Each individual action might be easy, but the value of an action depends on what you do ten steps later. You might take an action that looks useless in the moment but turns out to be the thing that unlocks the solution. So the credit assignment problem becomes much harder, and I think this is why reinforcement learning becomes almost unavoidable for agents. You need a signal that comes from the final outcome and propagates back to the decisions along the way, rather than imitating each step in isolation.

There's also a question of what happens in the model's head across those turns. Humans don't retain everything. If I've read a hundred files, I don't remember all of them verbatim, but I remember the structure and the few things that matter. I think agents need something similar. The context window is like working memory, and a long task will exceed it. So the model has to learn what to keep, what to summarize, and what to throw away. That ability to manage its own context over a long interaction is, in my view, one of the core capabilities, not an engineering detail on the side.

And I'd add one more thing. Multi-round interaction is also how the model recovers from mistakes. In a single turn, an error is fatal. In an agentic setting, you run the test, it fails, you read the error, and you fix it. So the standard for the model changes. It doesn't need to be right the first time. It needs to be good at noticing it's wrong and correcting course. I actually think that's a more realistic definition of intelligence than getting everything right in one shot.

r001.rationale: The response says the world’s response becomes new information, which the agent uses to update its understanding and decide what to do next.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that an agent doesn’t have to solve the entire problem in one shot. It can take an action, get feedback from the outside world, and then decide what to do next. That action might be searching for information, running code, or asking someone a question. Each interaction gives it new information that can change its approach.

So you can think of it as a loop: observe, reason, act, and then observe again. If I’m debugging a program, for example, I might start with a hypothesis, make a change, and run a test. If the test fails, that result helps me revise the hypothesis. The path to the solution emerges through those interactions.

The important capability is therefore more than producing a good answer at each step. It’s maintaining the overall objective, recognizing whether an action actually made progress, and adjusting when it didn’t. Multiple rounds are useful because they allow the agent to check its assumptions against the world.

r001.rationale: It says the agent receives feedback from an action and uses that information to decide what to do next, potentially changing its approach.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that an agent doesn’t have to solve the whole problem in a single response. It can take an action, observe what happens, and then decide what to do next. Each interaction gives it new information, which may change its understanding of the problem or its plan.

For example, if it’s writing code, it might first inspect the codebase, make a change, run the tests, and then use the errors to revise that change. The important thing is the loop: reasoning leads to action, action produces feedback, and feedback informs the next round of reasoning.

That also changes what we mean by intelligence. It’s not just whether the model can give a good answer immediately, but whether it can make progress over time—recognize a mistake, gather the information it needs, and keep working toward the goal. You need both a good next action and the ability to maintain direction across many actions.

r001.rationale: The response says the agent observes what happens after an action, and that this feedback informs its next round of reasoning and decisions.
